title: Contractor Profit Margin: What Is Normal?
description: Normal contractor profit margin explained: gross and net ranges by trade, markup vs margin math, and a worked job example.

cover.alt: Illustration of a rising chart on a for pros blueprint background with a measuring tape

tool.name: Markup vs margin
tool.short: Convert markup and margin, set a price

keywords: what is a good profit margin for a contractor
takeaways: Remodelers averaged a 29.9 percent gross margin and a 6.3 percent net margin in 2024, per NAHB.
A 30 percent markup is not a 30 percent margin. It gives you about a 23 percent margin.
Price from your own overhead first. A margin that works for a solo painter can sink a crew with a shop.
body:
A normal contractor profit margin is about 20 to 30 percent gross and 5 to 10 percent net for most small residential firms. Remodelers in NAHB data averaged 29.9 percent gross and 6.3 percent net in 2024, while the top quarter of construction firms in CFMA data cleared about 12 percent net. If your net sits below 5 percent month after month, the business is paying you less than the risk is worth.

## The short answer by firm type

Gross margin is what is left after direct job costs: labor, materials, subs, permits and rentals. Net margin is what is left after overhead too: insurance, truck, fuel, phone, software, rent, marketing and office help. Two firms can show the same gross margin and very different net margins.

| Firm type | Typical gross margin | Typical net margin |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Remodeler (NAHB average, 2024) | 29.9 percent | 6.3 percent |
| Construction firms overall (CFMA average) | About 20 to 22 percent | 6.7 percent |
| Top quarter of CFMA firms | Higher than average | About 12 percent |
| Healthy small contractor target | 25 to 40 percent | 8 to 15 percent |

Trade changes the picture. Licensed trades with service and repair work often hold higher margins because callers need help fast and fewer firms can do the work. General contractors who pass large sub costs through the books usually show lower gross margins on paper, even on good jobs. Compare your numbers with firms like yours, not with every contractor in the country. Our [markup vs margin calculator](/blog/markup-vs-margin-calculator/) turns a target margin into the markup you need on cost.

## Worked example: a $50,000 kitchen remodel

Say you sign a kitchen remodel at $50,000. Your direct costs come in on plan.

- Labor: $16,000
- Materials: $12,000
- Subcontractors: $7,000
- Direct costs total: $16,000 + $12,000 + $7,000 = $35,000
- Gross profit: $50,000 - $35,000 = $15,000
- Gross margin: $15,000 / $50,000 = 30 percent

Now take out overhead for the weeks this job ties up your crew. Say your share of insurance, truck, fuel, phone, software and office costs for this job is $11,800, which is 23.6 percent of the price.

- Net profit: $15,000 - $11,800 = $3,200
- Net margin: $3,200 / $50,000 = 6.4 percent

That 6.4 percent net lands right next to the NAHB remodeler average of 6.3 percent. The job looked like a 30 percent job at signing. It paid like a 6.4 percent job at the end, and both numbers are true.

Check the markup on the same job. Markup is profit divided by cost, not by price. Gross profit of $15,000 on $35,000 of direct cost is a 42.9 percent markup ($15,000 / $35,000). You needed a markup near 43 percent to land a 30 percent gross margin. If you had marked the job up by 30 percent instead, the price would have been $35,000 x 1.30 = $45,500, and your gross margin would have been $10,500 / $45,500, about 23 percent. That one mix-up costs real money on every bid. Run your own jobs through the [contractor hourly rate calculator](/blog/contractor-hourly-rate-calculator/) to see if your labor rate carries its share of overhead.

## Why is your margin lower than the bid?

Three leaks show up again and again. First, labor runs long. A two-day overrun on a three-person crew can eat the whole net profit on a mid-size job. Second, overhead gets guessed, not counted. Owners often leave out their own estimating time, tool replacement and vehicle wear, so the bid never had room for them. Third, change orders get done free. Small extras feel cheap one at a time, then add up to days of unpaid work.

Job costing is the fix that actually works. After each job, list what you spent on labor hours, materials, subs and rentals, then compare it with the bid line by line. You will find your leak within two or three jobs. Price the next bid with that leak closed. The [painting estimate calculator](/blog/painting-estimate-calculator/) shows the same habit in a trade format: every cost listed before a price comes out.

## What margin should you target?

Use this verdict. If you are a solo operator with low overhead, a net margin of 10 to 15 percent is a fair target. If you run crews, carry a shop and pay office help, hold net at 8 to 12 percent and treat anything under 5 percent as a warning. Gross margin has to be high enough to cover your real overhead and still leave that net. Work backward: add your overhead percent to your target net percent, and that sum is the gross margin your prices must produce.

Do not copy a competitor price and hope the margin follows. A firm with paid-off trucks and no rent can live on margins that would sink you. Your price has to fit your costs. If a job cannot carry your margin at a price the client will accept, the honest move is to pass on the job, not to shave the margin and hope volume saves you. Volume at a loss just makes the loss bigger.

One more check before you bid. Ask if the price still works when one thing goes wrong: a material price rise, a sick crew member, a permit delay. A healthy margin is the cushion that absorbs that one bad week. A thin margin means one bad week turns a busy month into a losing month.

## Frequently asked questions

### What is a good net profit margin for a small contractor?
Aim for 8 to 15 percent net. NAHB put the remodeler average at 6.3 percent in 2024, and the top quarter of CFMA firms reached about 12 percent, so 8 percent or better puts you ahead of the typical firm.

### Is a 20 percent markup the same as a 20 percent margin?
No. A 20 percent markup on $10,000 of cost gives a $12,000 price and $2,000 of profit. That profit is 16.7 percent of the price, so your margin is 16.7 percent, not 20 percent.

### What gross margin do remodelers average?
NAHB reported an average gross margin of 29.9 percent for remodelers in 2024, up from 24.9 percent in 2021. Cost of sales took the other 70.1 percent of revenue.

### Why is my gross margin fine but my net margin near zero?
Your overhead is eating the gap. Add up a full year of insurance, vehicle, fuel, phone, software, rent, marketing and your own unbillable time, then divide by revenue. Many small firms find overhead near 20 percent of revenue once they count it all.

### Should I lower my margin to win more bids?
Only with a clear reason and a floor you will not cross. Winning work below 5 percent net leaves no cushion for overruns, callbacks or slow months, and one bad job can erase a season of thin wins.

## Next step
Take your last three finished jobs and work out gross and net margin on each one. Then set your target margin and convert it to a markup with our [markup vs margin calculator](/blog/markup-vs-margin-calculator/) before your next bid goes out.
